Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
All Correct Answers: ["1963", "1956"]. Explanation: Document 1 is talking about the basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan, who was born on February 17, 1963, so 1963 is correct. Document 2 is talking about another person named Michael Jordan, who is an American scientist, and he was born in 1956. Therefore, the answer 1956 from Document 2 is also correct. Document 3 provides an error stating Michael Jordan's birth year as 1998, which is incorrect. Based on the correct information from Document 1, Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963. Document 4 does not provide any useful information.

Question: Which educational institution did Willy Schwabacher attend?
Document 1: As Willy Schwabacher delved deeper into the world of numismatics, his fascination with the intricacies of coin design and the stories they told only grew stronger. It was during his undergraduate years at the University of Nottingham, surrounded by the historic architecture and vibrant cultural scene of the East Midlands, that his passion truly began to take shape. Willy would often spend hours pouring over dusty tomes in the university's sprawling library, uncovering hidden gems and obscure references that shed new light on his research. His favorite haunt was the George Green Library, where the musty scent of old books and the soft hum of fluorescent lights created the perfect atmosphere for immersion. It was there, nestled between shelves stacked high with volumes on art history and archaeology, that he stumbled upon an obscure treatise on medieval coinage. The author, a little-known scholar named Dr. Emilia Fothergill, had a way of bringing the past to life with her vivid descriptions of 12th-century minting techniques and the rivalries between royal courts. Willy was captivated by her writing style, which seemed to dance across the page like the intricate patterns on a Byzantine solidus. He devoured the entire book in a single sitting, his mind racing with the possibilities of how he could apply Dr. Fothergill's theories to his own research. As the semester drew to a close, Willy decided to take a chance and reach out to Dr. Fothergill, hoping to discuss her work and perhaps even secure an introduction to the academic community. To his surprise, she responded promptly, inviting him to meet at the university's Department of Archaeology, where she was scheduled to deliver a guest lecture on the numismatic significance of the Crusades. The day of the lecture arrived, and Willy made his way to the department, his heart racing with excitement. As he entered the crowded seminar room, he spotted Dr. Fothergill, a statuesque woman with silver hair and piercing green eyes, standing at the podium. Her words were like a symphony, weaving together threads of history, politics, and art to create a rich tapestry that left the audience entranced. After the lecture, Willy mustered the courage to approach Dr. Fothergill, introducing himself and sharing his own research on the coinage of the Holy Roman Empire. To his delight, she was impressed by his knowledge and enthusiasm, offering words of encouragement and a valuable connection to the academic community.
Document 2: Title: The Numismatist's Academic Pursuits: Unveiling Willy Schwabacher's Connection to Technical University of Darmstadt

In the realm of numismatics, few names shine as brightly as Willy Schwabacher, a German numismatist whose contributions to the field are still revered today. While his expertise in coins and medals is well-documented, a lesser-known aspect of his life is his academic background. A crucial piece of evidence reveals that Schwabacher attended the prestigious Technical University of Darmstadt, a German institution renowned for its excellence in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields. This narrative delves into the life of Willy Schwabacher, exploring the context and significance of his connection to this esteemed university. Born in the late 19th century, Willy Schwabacher grew up in a Germany undergoing rapid industrialization and modernization. As a young man, he developed a fascination with coins and medals, which would eventually become his life's passion. However, before devoting himself fully to numismatics, Schwabacher recognized the importance of a solid education. In the early 20th century, he made the decision to enroll at the Technical University of Darmstadt, an institution that had been at the forefront of scientific and technological advancements since its founding in 1877. Founded during the reign of Grand Duke Ludwig IV of Hesse, the Technical University of Darmstadt was established to provide education and training in the fields of engineering, architecture, and natural sciences. By the time Schwabacher attended, the university had already gained a reputation for excellence, attracting students from across Germany and beyond. The university's strong emphasis on practical application and innovative research created an environment that fostered intellectual curiosity and creativity – qualities that would serve Schwabacher well in his future numismatic pursuits. Schwabacher's time at the Technical University of Darmstadt was marked by intense academic rigor and a deepening of his understanding of the natural sciences. His coursework in subjects like chemistry, physics, and mathematics provided a solid foundation for his later work in numismatics, where an understanding of metallurgy, materials science, and historical context was essential. The university's emphasis on experimentation and hands-on learning also instilled in Schwabacher a meticulous attention to detail, a trait that would become a hallmark of his numismatic research.
